```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using MatrixCommunityModels
using LinearAlgebra, Printf, Statistics
using Plots
```

## Eighteen annuals on serpentine

Godoy, Kraft & Levine (2014) sowed 18 annual plants of the serpentine grassland of the
Sedgwick Reserve, California, as focal plants into a density gradient of each species,
itself included, and measured their germination, the survival of their seed in the soil,
and the seed they set with and without neighbours. From these they built a model of each
pair of species competing for a season, and used the coexistence theory of Chesson (2012)
to split each pair's difference into a stabilising niche difference and an average fitness
difference. They asked whether close relatives differ less in either. This vignette builds
their model from its two stages, reproduces its niche and fitness differences and predicted
outcomes for every pair, checks them by simulation, and says where the result departs from
what the paper prints.

The model counts `N`, the seeds of species `i` in the soil before germination in year `t`
(Godoy et al. 2014, eqns. 1 and 2, after Chesson 1990 and Levine & HilleRisLambers 2009):

$$N_{i,t+1} = (1 - g_i) s_i N_{i,t} + g_i N_{i,t} \frac{\lambda_i}{1 + \sum_j \alpha_{ij} g_j N_{j,t}}.$$

A share `g` of the seeds germinates; the rest stay in the soil and survive the year with
probability `s`. A germinant sets `λ` seeds without neighbours, fewer when crowded by the
germinants `g_j N_j` of each species, each weighted by its interaction coefficient `α_ij`,
the per capita effect of a germinant of `j` on the seed set of `i`.

## Two stages

The model has one number per species, but it hides two kinds of seed: those that stay
dormant, which only survive, and those that germinate, which compete and set seed. Counted
just after germination, each species has two stages, `seeds` (the `(1 - g) N` dormant seeds)
and `plants` (the `g N` germinants). In a year a dormant seed survives with probability `s`,
and a germinant sets `λ / (1 + crowding)` seeds; next autumn every seed in the soil, old or
new, germinates with probability `g`. The sum of the two stages is the paper's `N`, year by
year. Crowding then reads the `plants` stage of every species directly: it is a pool.

`annual_plant` builds one species:

```{julia}
plant = annual_plant(:a; g = 0.1, s = 0.5, lambda = 100, alpha = [:a => 0.2])
net = system(plant)[:a]
println(transition_names(net))
to_matrix(net, context(net, [45.0, 5.0], (a_crowding = 1.0,), nothing))
```

Two transitions, `seed_survival` and `seed_production`, each with an entry to either stage,
and seed production divided by `1 + a_crowding`. The matrix has rank one: dormant seeds and
germinants differ only in what they bring to the next autumn's seed pool, `s` or
`λ / (1 + crowding)` seeds each, and that pool is then split in the same shares. Its one
non-zero eigenvalue, `(1 - g) s + g λ / (1 + crowding)`, is the paper's per capita growth
rate.

Each species adds its germinants, weighted by `α_ij`, to the crowding pool `<i>_crowding` of
every species `i` it competes with, itself included. Composing species joins their pools.

## The data

The authors deposited the vital rates and interaction coefficients on figshare (CC0), and
`ANNUAL_PLANTS_GODOY_2014` reads them from `data/annual_plants`:

```{julia}
p = ANNUAL_PLANTS_GODOY_2014
η = annual_plant_eta(p)
println("code  species                      λ          g       s      η")
for (k, code) in enumerate(p.codes)
    @printf("%-5s %-27s %9.2f  %6.4f  %5.3f  %8.2f\n", code, p.names[k], p.lambda[k], p.g[k], p.s[k], η[k])
end
```

`η = λ g / (1 - (1 - g) s)` is the seed produced per seed lost from the soil, to death or
germination, without competitors; every species persists alone. The paper's Appendix S2,
Table 3 prints the same rates. The germination fractions agree with it to the three
decimals printed and the seed survivals to the two printed, but not the seed set:

```{julia}
λ3 = [784.8, 1946.32, 289.91, 1146.23, 14606.58, 835.17, 295.73, 341.23, 1092.95, 60.92, 991.28, 3689.6,
      481.63, 1484.84, 287.72, 2814.96, 1393.34, 3234.13]
for k in sortperm(abs.(p.lambda .- λ3) ./ λ3; rev = true)[1:5]
    @printf("%-5s data %9.2f, Table 3 %9.2f (%+.1f%%)\n", p.codes[k], p.lambda[k], λ3[k], 100 * (p.lambda[k] / λ3[k] - 1))
end
```

Only `AGRE`, `AMME` and `LOPU` agree within one seed. The deposit is the authors'
own, posted three years after the paper; it may be a later fit. Everything below uses it.

Of the 324 interaction coefficients, 66 are missing ("little confidence in the estimate",
says the deposit). The paper filled a missing coefficient with the product `r_i e_j` of the
responding species' common competitive response and the other's common competitive effect,
fitted to all the data at once (Appendix S4), whose values it prints (Appendix S2, Table 2).
`annual_plant_alphas` does the same:

```{julia}
A = annual_plant_alphas(p)
println("missing: ", count(isnan, p.alpha), "; on the diagonal: ", count(isnan, diag(p.alpha)))
@printf("ANAR on AGHE, alpha[1, 4], filled with r_AGHE e_ANAR = %.3f × %.3f = %.5f\n",
        p.response[1], p.effect[4], A[1, 4])
```

## One pair: a star thistle and a tarweed

*Centaurea melitensis* (`ceme`) and *Hemizonia congesta* (`heco`) are both Asteraceae.
`annual_plant_community` composes the two with their coefficients:

```{julia}
c = annual_plant_community(p; codes = (:ceme, :heco))
println(c)
n0 = vcat(annual_plant_state(:ceme, 1.0), annual_plant_state(:heco, 1000.0))
sol = project(c, n0, fill(nothing, 300))
seeds(sp) = vec(sum(sol[sp]; dims = 2))
plot(sol.t, [seeds(:ceme) seeds(:heco)]; label = ["C. melitensis" "H. congesta"], yscale = :log10,
     xlabel = "year", ylabel = "seeds in the soil before germination", lw = 2, size = (700, 350))
```

Starting from one seed, the star thistle invades the tarweed and the two settle together.
The equilibrium is where each species' growth rate is one, `1 + Σ_j α_ij P_j = η_i` for the
germinants `P`, a pair of linear equations; Newton's method on the composed community
(`periodic_point`) finds it and its stability:

```{julia}
i, j = 5, 11
P = A[[i, j], [i, j]] \ (η[[i, j]] .- 1)
e = periodic_point(c, sol.u[end, :], nothing)
@printf("germinants: linear solve %.4f, %.4f; composed nets %.4f, %.4f\n", P..., e.n[2], e.n[4])
@printf("largest multiplier %.4f\n", maximum(abs.(e.multipliers)))
```

## Niche and fitness differences

For this model, Godoy & Levine (2014) showed that the niche overlap of species `i` and `j` is

$$\rho = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{ij}\alpha_{ji}}{\alpha_{jj}\alpha_{ii}}},$$

the stabilising niche difference `1 - ρ`, and the average fitness ratio

$$\frac{\kappa_j}{\kappa_i} = \frac{\eta_j - 1}{\eta_i - 1}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{ij}\alpha_{ii}}{\alpha_{jj}\alpha_{ji}}}$$

(Godoy et al. 2014, eqns. 3 and 4), and that both species invade when rare, so that they
coexist, if `ρ < κ_j/κ_i < 1/ρ` (eqn. 5). That condition is the invasion criterion itself.
A species alone settles with `(η_j - 1)/α_jj` germinants, and a rare species `i` then grows
by `(1 - g_i) s_i + g_i λ_i / (1 + α_ij (η_j - 1)/α_jj)` a year, which exceeds one exactly when
`κ_j/κ_i < 1/ρ`. The composed nets give the same rate through `invasion_growth_rate`, with the
resident at its equilibrium:

```{julia}
alone(k) = (m = findfirst(==(k), p.codes); annual_plant_state(k, (η[m] - 1) / A[m, m] / p.g[m]))
ce, he = subcommunity(c, :ceme), subcommunity(c, :heco)
pairs = annual_plant_pairs(p)
x = only(filter(x -> x.i === :ceme && x.j === :heco, pairs))
@printf("C. melitensis invading:  nets %.12f, formula %.12f\n", invasion_growth_rate(ce, he, alone(:heco), nothing), x.invasion_i)
@printf("H. congesta invading:    nets %.12f, formula %.12f\n", invasion_growth_rate(he, ce, alone(:ceme), nothing), x.invasion_j)
@printf("rho %.4f, niche difference %.4f, fitness ratio kappa_heco/kappa_ceme %.4f\n", x.rho, x.niche_difference, x.fitness_ratio)
```

`annual_plant_pairs` gives these for all 153 pairs. When `ρ > 1` a species limits the other
more than itself; neither can then invade the other if their fitnesses are close enough
(`1/ρ < κ_j/κ_i < ρ`), and whichever is commoner wins, a priority effect.

```{julia}
count_outcome(o) = count(x -> x.outcome === o, pairs)
println("coexistence: ", count_outcome(:coexistence), ", exclusion: ", count_outcome(:exclusion),
        ", priority effect: ", count_outcome(:priority_effect))
println("rho > 1 in ", count(x -> x.rho > 1, pairs), " pairs (",
        round(Int, 100 * count(x -> x.rho > 1, pairs) / length(pairs)), "%)")
fitter(x) = max(x.fitness_ratio, 1 / x.fitness_ratio)
println("relaxed criterion 0.9 rho < kappa_i/kappa_j: ", count(x -> 0.9x.rho < 1 / fitter(x), pairs), " pairs")
for x in filter(x -> x.outcome === :coexistence, pairs)
    @printf("  %-4s %-4s  1 - rho = %6.3f   kappa_j/kappa_i = %7.3f   filled %d\n", x.i, x.j, x.niche_difference, x.fitness_ratio, x.filled)
end
```

The usual picture plots each pair's fitness ratio, taken as at least one, against its niche
difference. Pairs between the curve `κ = 1/ρ` and the axis coexist; pairs with `ρ > 1` (a
negative niche difference) between the dashed line `κ = ρ` and the axis have a priority effect.
Twelve pairs, with `1 - ρ` from -1.6 down to -7.1, lie off the left edge; all are exclusions or
priority effects:

```{julia}
nd = [x.niche_difference for x in pairs]
fr = [fitter(x) for x in pairs]
colour = Dict(:coexistence => :forestgreen, :exclusion => :grey55, :priority_effect => :firebrick)
plt = plot(; xlabel = "stabilising niche difference 1 - ρ", ylabel = "fitness ratio (fitter / less fit)",
           yscale = :log10, legend = :topleft, size = (700, 450), xlims = (-1.6, 1))
for o in (:exclusion, :priority_effect, :coexistence)
    k = [x.outcome === o for x in pairs]
    scatter!(plt, nd[k], fr[k]; label = replace(String(o), "_" => " "), color = colour[o], ms = 4, msw = 0)
end
d = range(-1.6, 0.995; length = 400)
plot!(plt, d, 1 ./ (1 .- d); color = :black, label = "κ = 1/ρ")
plot!(plt, d[d .<= 0], (1 .- d[d .<= 0]); color = :black, ls = :dash, label = "κ = ρ")
plt
```

Godoy et al. print three summaries of this analysis, and none is reproduced from the
deposited data. They find 12 of the 153 pairs predicted to coexist, against 10 here; 18
under the relaxed criterion, against 11; and interspecific effects above intraspecific in
15% of pairs, against `ρ > 1` in 37% here. Their Fig. 5 shows the phylogenetic distances of
their 12 coexisting pairs: one near 190 million years, five near 260, three near 275 and
three near 305, with a mean of 270.58. On the dated tree of their Appendix S3, the 10 pairs
here lie at 190.9 (one), 258.2 to 260.4 (five), 274.7 (one) and 308.2 (three), with a mean
of 268.8. So the 10 pairs look like 10 of their 12, and the two missing pairs both lie near
275 million years. One candidate is *Euphorbia peplus* and *Lotus purshianus* (274.7), the
one pair that coexists under the relaxed criterion but not under eqn. 5 here (`EUPE` invades,
`LOPU` falls short). Neither the way the paper filled pairs with two missing coefficients,
nor the seed sets of its Table 3, nor reading the coefficient matrix transposed, gives 12;
the differences most likely lie in the coefficients, which the paper does not print.

Three things point to the deposit not being the set of coefficients behind the 2014 paper.
It was posted in March 2017 for a later paper (Saavedra et al. 2017, which cites its
version 1). In the paper the seed set without neighbours, `λ`, is fitted in the same model
as each target species' coefficients, and the deposited `λ` differs from Table 3. And Kraft,
Godoy & Levine (2015), on the same experiment, state that only 102 of the 153 pairs could be
fitted, and plot those 102 pairs with the same 12 coexisting (their Fig. S3). That figure has
many more pairs with large niche differences than these data do, and about a third of its
pairs at a niche difference of zero, against the 15% in the 2014 text. These data give 97
pairs with all four coefficients, or 125 if the coefficients estimated at zero count as
fitted. Version 1 of the deposit gives 33 coefficients as 0 and 33 as missing; the current
version gives all 66 as missing, and that is what is used here. Keeping the zeros gives 17
coexisting pairs, not 12. Neither the raw field data nor the fitting code is public.

## Simulated outcomes

The predicted outcomes rest on invasion when rare. To check them by simulation, each
species of each pair starts as a single seed against the other at its equilibrium alone,
and the composed community is run for 2000 years. The rare species has invaded if it ends
with more seeds than it began with:

```{julia}
function invades(i, j)
    c = annual_plant_community(p; codes = (i, j))
    n0 = vcat(annual_plant_state(i, 1.0), alone(j))
    sol = project(c, n0, fill(nothing, 2000))
    return sum(sol[i][end, :]) > 1
end
simulated = [(invades(x.i, x.j), invades(x.j, x.i)) for x in pairs]
predicted = [(x.invasion_i > 1, x.invasion_j > 1) for x in pairs]
println("pairs whose simulated invasions match the prediction: ", count(simulated .== predicted), " of ", length(pairs))
```

Every pair behaves as predicted, including the slowest: *Erodium cicutarium* invades *Lotus
wrangelianus* at a rate of 1.00034 a year (its seed bank barely decays, `s = 1`), and
*Hemizonia congesta* fails to invade *Agoseris retrorsa* at 0.99927. The coexisting pairs
settle at their equilibria, all stable:

```{julia}
for x in filter(x -> x.outcome === :coexistence, pairs)
    i, j = findfirst(==(x.i), p.codes), findfirst(==(x.j), p.codes)
    P = A[[i, j], [i, j]] \ (η[[i, j]] .- 1)
    c = annual_plant_community(p; codes = (x.i, x.j))
    n = vcat(annual_plant_state(x.i, P[1] / p.g[i]), annual_plant_state(x.j, P[2] / p.g[j]))
    e = periodic_point(c, 1.05 .* n, nothing)
    @printf("  %-4s %-4s germinants %8.2f %8.2f   largest multiplier %.5f\n", x.i, x.j, e.n[2], e.n[4], maximum(abs.(e.multipliers)))
end
```

## All eighteen together: competitive ranks

The paper ranked the species by competitive ability in a second way: simulate all 18
together; the species that excludes all others takes the top rank; run again without it;
species that coexist share a rank. The coefficients among all 18 are needed, the missing
ones filled as above. Here each round runs 20000 years from 100 seeds of each species, and
the survivors are those within a factor of 1000 of the most abundant:

```{julia}
function ranks(p; years = 20000)
    left, r, out = collect(p.codes), 0, Dict{Symbol, Int}()
    while !isempty(left)
        r += 1
        c = annual_plant_community(p; codes = left)
        n0 = reduce(vcat, [annual_plant_state(k, 100.0) for k in left])
        sol = project(c, n0, fill(nothing, years))
        N = [sum(sol[k][end, :]) for k in left]
        top = left[N .> 1e-3 * maximum(N)]
        foreach(k -> out[k] = r, top)
        filter!(k -> !(k in top), left)
    end
    return [out[k] for k in p.codes]
end
mine = ranks(p)
# ranks read by eye from the paper's Fig. 2
fig2 = [4, 2, 6, 9, 3, 4, 10, 6, 5, 10, 3, 8, 7, 5, 5, 6, 1, 3]
for k in sortperm(mine)
    @printf("  %-4s %-26s here %2d   Fig. 2 %2d\n", p.codes[k], p.names[k], mine[k], fig2[k])
end
tiedrank(v) = [mean(findall(==(x), sort(v))) for x in v]
@printf("Spearman correlation of the ranks: %.3f\n", cor(tiedrank(mine), tiedrank(fig2)))
```

The order is close to the paper's but not the same (a rank correlation of 0.87). Both put
*Plantago erecta* first, *Agoseris retrorsa* second, *Centaurea melitensis* and *Salvia
columbariae* third and *Agoseris heterophylla* fourth, and both put the two Geraniaceae and
*Anagallis arvensis* at the bottom. Here *Hemizonia congesta* survives the first round with
*P. erecta* (the pair coexists, with the largest niche difference of the coexisting pairs,
`1 - ρ = 0.93`), where the paper puts it third; *Clarkia purpurea* falls from fourth to
tenth; and the order runs to 13 groups here against 10 in the figure, since fewer pairs
coexist.

## What matches and what does not

Reproduced:

- the model of eqns. 1 and 2 as two-stage nets joined by crowding pools: the seeds of
  every run agree with the paper's one-stage recursion written in base R
  (`test/reference/R/run_annualplants_reference.R`) to rounding (about 1e-16), for pairs and
  for all 18 species;
- the niche overlaps, fitness ratios, invasion growth rates and predicted outcomes of all
  153 pairs, against the same R code, to about 1e-16; the invasion growth rates of the
  composed nets equal the formula;
- the predicted outcomes, by simulation of every pair from each species rare, and the
  coexistence equilibria, all stable;
- the germination fractions and seed survivals of Table 3, at its printed precision.

Not reproduced:

- the seed set without neighbours of Table 3, which differs from the deposited values by up
  to 25% (*Centaurea melitensis*);
- the paper's counts: 12 coexisting pairs (10 here), 18 under the relaxed criterion (11),
  and 15% of pairs with stronger interspecific than intraspecific effects (37% with `ρ > 1`);
  the phylogenetic distances of the coexisting pairs suggest the 10 are among the paper's 12;
- the competitive ranks of Fig. 2, read by eye, which agree in outline only.

None of these mismatches traces to the model or its code: the equations here and in the R
reference follow eqns. 1 to 5 of the paper term by term, and the coefficient matrix is read
with rows as the responding species, as the file name says.

The paper's regressions on phylogenetic distance, and its permutation and bootstrap tests,
are not repeated; the phylogenetic distances quoted above were computed from the Newick tree
printed in Appendix S3, which is not shipped. The paper was read in full as its accepted
manuscript with appendices (CSIC repository); its figures were read from the rendered pages.
